chapter.title: Plato and Aristotle: is the real world the one we see?

cards.body: A teacher and his student spent 20 years at the same school in Athens, and they still disagreed about whether the table in front of them was the real thing. Plato, the teacher, said every table you touch is a rough copy of a perfect *Table* you can only reach by thinking. At our long dinner table, Aristotle is the next guest to speak, and for a loyal student his reply is a surprise: **look harder at the actual table**.
cards.simpler: Plato was a teacher and Aristotle was his student. They spent 20 years at the same school in Athens. Still, they disagreed about the table right in front of them. Plato said any table you can touch is a rough copy of a perfect *Table*, one you can only reach by thinking. At our long dinner table, Aristotle speaks next. You'd expect a loyal student to agree. Instead he says: **look harder at the actual table**.

cards.prompt: Some people have been chained in a cave since birth, facing a wall. A fire behind them throws shadows of passing objects onto it: a jug, a horse. You ask them what's real. What do they say?

options.text: Nothing, because they know it's a trick.

whyNot.b: That's what you'd find if you turned round. They've never seen the fire, so they can't name it.
whyNot.c: That's knowing it's a trick, and you need something outside to compare with before you can know that. They have nothing outside.

cards.reteach: If shadows are all you've ever seen, shadows are your whole world. You'd name them and study them. Nothing would look missing.

cards.title: Plato's cave
cards.body:
That cave is Plato's. It comes from his book the *Republic*. One prisoner is set free. He turns round, the fire dazzles him, and then he's dragged up and out into sunlight. Slowly he sees real horses, real trees, and at last the sun itself.

Plato says we are the prisoners. The objects carried past the fire are the ordinary things around us, and the shadows are copies of them. The things outside are *Forms*, Plato's word for the perfect pattern a thing copies, like perfect Justice or the perfect Circle. The sun stands for the highest Form of all, the Good. So the world we see is made of **copies of something more real**, and you reach the real things by thinking, not by looking.

When the freed man goes back down to tell the others, they laugh at him and threaten to kill him. That's a quiet nod to Socrates, Plato's teacher.
cards.simpler: This cave is from Plato's book the *Republic*. One prisoner is set free. The fire dazzles him. Then he's dragged into sunlight and sees real trees, real horses, and the sun. Plato says we are the prisoners. The objects carried past the fire are ordinary things, and the shadows are copies of them. The things outside are *Forms*: perfect patterns, like perfect Justice or a perfect Circle. The sun is the highest Form, the Good. So what we see are **copies of something more real**, reached by thinking. When he goes back, the others laugh and threaten to kill him, a nod to Socrates, Plato's teacher.

cards.title: The napkin circle
cards.body: Priya draws a circle on a café napkin to show how big the pizza should be. It wobbles, the pen skips, and one side comes out flat. Nobody has ever drawn a perfect circle, not even with a compass, once you look under a microscope. Yet everyone at the table knows exactly what that wobbly line is failing to be. For Plato, that's the clue: **you know the perfect circle without ever having seen one**, so it must exist somewhere, just not on the napkin.
cards.simpler: Priya draws a circle on a café napkin to show the pizza size. It wobbles, the pen skips, and one side goes flat. Nobody has ever drawn a perfect circle. Even one made with a compass looks bumpy under a microscope. Yet everyone at the table knows what Priya's line was trying to be. Plato saw a clue in that: **you know the perfect circle without ever having seen one**, so it must exist somewhere, just not on the napkin.

cards.prompt: Three friends argue about what makes a good friend. Which one is thinking like Plato?

options.text: Maya lists ten good friends she's had and looks for what they share.
Leo says every friendship falls short of a perfect Friendship you can only grasp by thinking.
Ben says 'friend' is just a word, so it means whatever you like.

whyNot.a: That's learning from examples you can see, which is the student's move, not Plato's. To Plato, examples are shadows.
whyNot.c: That's a shrug, not Plato. He thought there was one perfect answer out there.

cards.reteach: For Plato, the friendships you can see are shadows on the cave wall. The Form of Friendship is the real thing outside the cave. You reach it by thinking, not by collecting more examples.

cards.title: Aristotle pulls it down to earth
cards.body:
Aristotle studied at Plato's school, the Academy, for about 20 years. You'd expect him to build on his teacher's idea. Instead **he brought the Forms down into things themselves**. What makes an oak an oak isn't in another world. It's in the acorn, the bark, the way the tree grows.

So you find it by looking. Aristotle spent time on the island of Lesbos studying sea creatures, cutting animals open and sorting them into groups.

About 1,800 years later, the painter Raphael put the two side by side: Plato points at the sky, and Aristotle holds his hand flat over the ground. The whole argument, one gesture each.
cards.simpler: Aristotle studied at Plato's school, the Academy, for about 20 years. Yet instead of following his teacher, **he brought the Forms down into things themselves**. What makes an oak an oak is in the acorn, the bark, how it grows. You find it by looking. On the island of Lesbos he studied sea creatures, cutting them open and sorting them. Some 1,800 years later, Raphael painted the pair: Plato pointing at the sky, Aristotle's hand flat over the ground.

cards.body: After rewatching *The Matrix*, Sam tells everyone that Plato thought the world was fake. Not quite. A shadow is a real shadow. Plato just ranked it lower, as a copy of something better. When someone says Plato called the world an illusion, listen for the missing word: **copy, not fake**.
cards.simpler: After rewatching *The Matrix*, Sam tells everyone that Plato thought the world was fake. That's not quite right. A shadow is still a real shadow. Plato just ranked it lower, as a copy of something better. Think of a photo of a friend: the photo is real, but it isn't the friend. So when someone says Plato called the world an illusion, listen for the missing word: **copy, not fake**.

cards.prompt: A scientist tests a new drug on 2,000 patients and changes her mind when the results come in. Whose side of the table is she on?

options.text: Plato's: you reach the truth by thinking past what you see.
Aristotle's: you find the truth by looking closely at the world.
Neither: scientists stay out of philosophy.

whyNot.a: That's Plato's climb out of the cave, not her method. She trusts what she can measure.
whyNot.c: That's stepping outside the long argument. Her method is itself a reply, and it echoes Aristotle.

cards.reteach: Ask where each of them goes to find the truth. Plato looks away from the senses, toward perfect Forms. Aristotle looks more closely at the thing in front of him, just as she did with 2,000 patients.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Plato said what we see are shadows on a cave wall, and the real things are perfect Forms that you reach by thinking. Aristotle, his student for 20 years, said the Forms live inside things, so **look closely at the world and you'll find them**.
cards.simpler: Plato said the things we see are shadows on a cave wall. The real things are perfect Forms, and you reach them by thinking. Aristotle was his student for 20 years, but he said the Forms live inside things. So **look closely at the world and you'll find them**.

cards.body:
Tonight, pick one object near you, like a mug. Write one sentence about it the way Plato would, then one the way Aristotle would. Notice which one came more easily.

Tomorrow: in 1641, one man doubts everything and finds exactly one thing he can't.
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick one object near you, like a mug. First write one sentence about it the way Plato would, thinking about the perfect mug it copies. Then write one the way Aristotle would, looking closely at the mug in your hand. Notice **which sentence came more easily**. Tomorrow: in 1641, one man doubts everything and finds exactly one thing he can't doubt.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now tell the cave story in 3 sentences and say whether a scientist sits closer to Plato or Aristotle.

dubious_claims: Card 1: 'walked out disagreeing with his teacher': Aristotle left Athens after Plato died in 347 BC. He didn't walk out of the school, and card 4 says this itself, so the two cards contradict each other.
Card 3: 'The sun is a form': in the Republic the sun stands for the Form of the Good, and the objects outside the cave are the forms.

Card 8, option c feedback: 'the one thing they shared' suggests they agreed on politics. They didn't: Aristotle attacks Plato's Republic in Politics Book II. The feedback also never says what the shared thing is.
Card 8 is labelled 'recall' and says 'from this chapter', but the painting (Raphael's School of Athens) is never mentioned in the chapter. The reader has to work out the answer from the gestures.
Open loop: the 1641 teaser is in the second-to-last card. The chapter actually ends on the try card's 'That's Plato's question.'
repairedFrom.why: The core teach card gets the cave's key mapping wrong: the shadows are copies of copies (the puppets are the ordinary things), and the sun is the Form of the Good, the highest form, not just 'a form', so the reader learns a muddled version of the chapter's central idea.
repairedFrom.fix: Replace 'The shadows are ordinary things. The sun is a form' with 'The puppets are ordinary things and the shadows are copies of them; the things outside are forms, Plato's word for the perfect pattern a thing copies, and the sun is the highest form of all.'
